original_body: The day before: separate the eggs and slip each yolk into a small dish, whole.
Pour the soy sauce and mirin over, so the yolks are just covered. Cover and refrigerate 24 hours. They turn deep amber and firm up like soft jam.
Use eggs sold for eating raw, or pasteurised ones. Keep the cured yolks cold and use them within two days.

ingredients: Ground pork, or pork and beef
original_body: Put the meat, soy, sugar, sake, mirin and ginger in a cold pan and stir them together before the heat goes on. That keeps the crumbs fine.
Cook over medium heat, stirring all the time with four chopsticks held together, until the liquid has gone and the meat is fine, glossy and just dry, 6–8 minutes.
Bongo's favourite: a spoon of soboro with one soy-cured yolk on top.
Cut the pork belly into 2 cm pieces. Fry it in the sesame oil over high heat until it browns, about 2 minutes.
Add the squeezed kimchi and fry 1 minute more, until the pan is dry. Wet kimchi soaks the rice and the onigiri falls apart. Let it cool.
Cut the soft kombu left from making dashi into thin strips, about 3 cm long.
Simmer with the water, soy, sugar, mirin and vinegar over low heat, stirring now and then, until the liquid is gone and the kombu is glossy, 15–20 minutes.
Off the heat, stir in the shiso, cut into fine strips. It keeps a week in the fridge.
Chop the takana finely and squeeze out as much liquid as you can.
Fry it in the sesame oil with the chilli over medium-high heat for 2–3 minutes, add the soy and cook until dry. Stir in the sesame seeds.
Toast the peanuts in a dry pan over medium-low heat until fragrant, 2–3 minutes.
Stir the miso, sugar, mirin and water together, pour it over the peanuts and stir over low heat until the miso turns glossy and clings to every nut, 2 minutes.
Spread on a plate to cool. It sets sticky; break it up before using.
Cut the eggplants into 1 cm dice, toss with the salt and leave 10 minutes. Squeeze them hard.
Fry in the oil over medium heat until soft, 4 minutes. Add the soy, sugar and sake and cook, stirring, until the liquid is gone and the eggplant is dark and glossy, about 6 minutes.
Nigihaya mixes its eggplant all through the rice instead of hiding it in the middle. Do the same: fold it into warm rice, then shape.
Put the olive oil and garlic in a small cold pan and warm it over low heat until the garlic is pale gold, 4–5 minutes. Darker garlic turns bitter.
Off the heat, add the chilli flakes and salt. Fold the oil and garlic through the rice before shaping, about 1 tsp per onigiri.
Slit the mentaiko sac and scrape the roe out of its skin.
Stir it with the mayo, then fold in the cream cheese cubes without breaking them.

original_notes: Bongo's signature is sujiko, salt-cured salmon roe still in its membrane. Other fillings you just buy: negitoro (chopped fatty tuna with scallion, eat within the hour), salmon with mentaiko on top, grilled tarako with mentai mayo (Togoshi-ya), and Yadoroku's kazunoko in sake lees (herring roe) and ami tsukudani (tiny shrimp simmered in sweet soy).
In spring Bongo also has fuki miso, butterbur stems chopped and fried with miso and sugar. The peanut miso in step 6 is the year-round cousin.
Nigihaya in Kyoto uses its family's Marizuke, eggplant salted for two years and then simmered. Step 7 is a quick version of the idea, not their recipe.
Soboro, shiso kombu, takana and peanut miso keep 4–5 days in the fridge. Pork kimchi keeps two days.
